title: Best aluminium bikes 2026 reviewed
content:
Cyclist
Best aluminium bikes 2026 reviewed

The best aluminium bikes are better today than they’ve ever been, rivalling and in some cases beating similarly priced carbon bikes for overall performance and value.

Since carbon became the default material from which to make competitive road race and gravel racing bikes, steel has forged a second life for itself. However, if steel is vinyl – outmoded but charming – then aluminium has risked becoming an eight-track cassette tape – an unloved evolutionary stepping-stone doomed to the charity shop of history.

It wasn’t always so. For around a decade from the mid-90s to the early-2000s, aluminium was the material of choice, with Miguel Indurain being the first to win the Tour de France aboard an aluminium bike, a Pinarello, in 1995.

However, with Lance Armstrong ‘winning’ on a carbon Trek OCLV Madone only three years later, aluminium has often since found itself largely consigned to brands’ entry-level machines.

Don’t discount the metal option though. We’ve picked seven aluminium bikes that highlight the continuing appeal of aluminium.

Reviews of the best aluminium road bikes and gravel bikes

  1. Boardman SLR 8.8: RRP £875 – Read our full review
  2. Cannondale CAAD14 3: RRP: £2,500
  3. Canyon Endurace AllRoad: RRP £1,099
  4. Condor Italia RC Disc: RRP £1,299 (frameset) – Read our full review
  5. Specialized Allez: RRP £1,000 – Read our full review
  6. Specialized Allez Sprint: RRP £2,600 – Read our full review
  7. Sonder Camino AL gravel bike: RRP £1,818.99 – Read our full review

Should I buy an aluminium bike?

You certainly shouldn’t rule aluminium out, particularly if you’re spending less than £3,000 / $3,500.

Aluminium has been enjoying a revival, with new manufacturing methods once again making it a viable choice for race-winning bikes (or just plain fun ones). Aluminium bikes can be stiff, zippy and very light.

A note on nomenclature, by the way: aluminium is often referred to as ‘alloy’ which is strictly speaking quite vague, since all metal-framed bikes are made from alloys of one sort or another.

Are aluminium bikes harsh?

They can be, but they don’t have to be. The ultra-stiff aluminium race bikes of the nineties and 2000s gave the material a reputation for harsh ride quality, but how a bike rides depends on multiple factors including frame design, spec choices and tyre pressure.

The best aluminium frames build in some vertical flex for comfort, typically with skinny or dropped seatstays or flexible seatposts. The trend towards wider tyres has helped here too – many road bikes now come with 28mm tyres as standard and can accept wider ones still.

Aluminium can also handle the rough and tumble (we hope not too much of the latter) of gravel better than carbon too, tending to dent rather than break if it takes a hit.

How we test and why you should trust our advice

Our team of expert testers led by tech editor Sam Challis has an immense combined experience of riding everything from the very cheapest entry-level bikes, up to the latest and greatest flagship superbikes.

We’re riders just like you who love cycling for the joy, the excitement, and the physical challenge and we review bikes by putting in the miles in all weathers. We value bikes that are at once easy to live with and a pleasure to ride, and we admire brands that dare to be different or that offer a particularly compelling package for the money.

We will never recommend a bike we wouldn’t spend our own money on.

The best aluminium bikes reviewed

Boardman SLR 8.8

£875 | Buy here

  • Pros: Smoothly welded frame, tubeless ready wheels
  • Cons: External cables, some cheaper drivetrain components, relatively heavy

Boardman has long been a leader on value and the SLR 8.8 is a fantastic introduction to road cycling, with a nicely finished aluminium frame that looks remarkably carbon-esque.

Price well below a grand, there are some spec compromises in the form of cable disc brakes (as opposed to hydraulics) and a crankset that doesn’t match the Shimano Tiagra drivetrain, but nothing that stops this being a solid buy.

The SLR 8.8 is fun and engaging despite being at the heavier end of the road bike spectrum. The brakes may be basic but they offer plenty of confidence, while a generous range of gears will get you up most hills.

For a little more cash, the Shimano 105-equipped Boardman SLR 8.9 is also worth a look.

  • Read our full Boardman SLR 8.8 review

Cannondale CAAD14 3

£2,500 | Buy here

  • Pros: Looks good, lightweight, smooth riding
  • Cons: Pricey, aggressive ride position may not suit all riders

Cannondale was famous during the ’90s for its slinky-looking CAAD frames, which are still objects of lust for a particular breed of bike nerd. Having diverged from the older CAAD aesthetic with previous generations, the latest CAAD14 returns to a classic double diamond frame and oversized tubing.

It’s lovely-looking and lighter than many carbon competitors, while its chunky looking tubing should also provide a ride far smoother than you’d imagine possible. The CAAD14 1 halo bike is stunning and boasts a 7.9kg claimed weight.

Tyre clearance is now 32mm and the Delta steerer, ported over from the carbon SuperSix Evo offers full cable integration. There are just three specs on offer, with this Shimano 105 mechanical option the least expensive.

Canyon Endurace AllRoad

£1,099 | Buy here

  • Pros: Great spec for its price, 40mm tyre clearance
  • Cons: Single spec only

The Endurace is no longer just one bike, there are four Endurace platforms, with the Endurace AllRoad the sole alloy representative. It’s a brilliant value alloy road bike with 40mm tyre clearance and fitted with grippy 35mm tyres, so it can handle light off-road as well as on-road and commuting duties.

A carbon fork helps keep things smooth at the front, internal cables keep them neat, while mudguard and top tube bag mounts add versatility. Canyon fits a wide-range Shimano CUES 10-speed groupset, complete with hydraulic disc brakes, adding yet more versatility.

Condor Italia RC Disc

£1,399.99 (frame only) | Buy here

  • Pros: Great looks, spec built to order, now with disc brakes
  • Cons: Limited availability, racy geometry may not suit some riders

London cycling stalwart Condor produces its range in Italy. The race-oriented Italia RC is a legitimately fast bike with a moderate price tag, ideal for regular racing and fast training.

Featuring an asymmetric down tube with a flattened profile to resist twisting, it should be happy to get thrown about.

Having previous eschewed anything as crassly modern as disc brakes or bolt-thru axles, this latest version sports both. Thankfully the Italia is still gorgeous to look at in deep two-tone blue.

The Italia is sold frame-only, and Condor will help build the bike up to match your requirements. You can also call on the experience of its in-house fitters to get it spot on.

  • Read our Condor Italia RC review (rim brake version)

Specialized Allez Sport

£1,600 | Buy here

  • Pros: Disc brakes and wide tyre clearance
  • Cons: Significantly more expensive than its predecessor, wheels need upgrading

The Specialized Allez had a major update in 2023, its first since 2017. Gone are the rim brakes in favour of disc brakes, while tyre clearance has increased to 35mm, both putting the Allez in line with modern trends.

The base model Allez has a Shimano Claris 8-speed groupset and mechanical disc brakes, but you’ll need to pay almost 50% more for the higher spec Allez Sport, which we reviewed, and which has a 10-speed Shimano Tiagra groupset with hydraulic disc brakes.

It’s a durable bike with a weight just shy of 10kg. A good proportion of that heft is in the wheels and tyres though, which feel due for an upgrade to improve the Allez’s performance.

  • Read our full Specialized Allez review

Specialized Allez Sprint

£2,600 | Buy here

  • Pros: Aero alloy frame, stiff and responsive
  • Cons: Ride position is quite aggressive, expensive for alloy

The standard Allez is Specialized’s entry-level, do-it-all road bike while the Sprint is a hardcore racer created to showcase the brand’s aluminium construction technology, and provide a real alternative to carbon.

The Allez Sprint is very sculpted for an aluminium frame, employing SmartWeld technology to produce an aero-tested frame that’s effectively a metal version of the Specialized Tarmac.

In fact, many features are nicked from the Tarmac including the geometry, and while the Allez’s frame is a good bit heavier its 1.5kg weight is still respectable enough.

The Allez Sprint is a stiff and lively bike, and we found a lot to like when we reviewed it.

Sonder Camino AL

£1,818.99 | Buy here

  • Pros: Wide tyre clearance, stable over rough ground, great value, broad spec choices
  • Cons: Stock bars are a little too flared, sedate on tarmac

Sonder’s Camino AL has room for 50mm gravel tyres and, as standard, is fitted with 45mm rubber, which ensures plenty of grip off-road, as well as a degree of cushioning from uneven surfaces, so that you’re not likely to be slowed down by roots and rocks. The Camino’s geometry offers stability on slippery tracks and when descending, although this does lead to a sedate ride when you need to link in tarmac sections.

All specs are now 1x, with either a SRAM or Shimano groupset, including electronic shifting options. The low base price leaves plenty for room for the extensive range of upgrades available, including Sonder’s own carbon wheels, a dropper seatpost and even a RockShox suspension fork. Sonder’s build-to-order approach allows you to choose crank and stem lengths and a range of saddles too.

The only change we’d make to the reviewed spec is a swap to the less flared Hurricane bars, as the Bomber bars’ very angled drops leave you resting on the edge of the levers, rather than the tops, which are broader.
